title: Room Acoustics and Cognitive Load when Listening to Speech
research_question: To investigate the effects of background noise or a long reverberation time in learning situations on the ability to identify, understand, and remember auditory information, and whether these effects increase cognitive load and impair memory, even when speech intelligibility is above threshold.

participants.description: Multiple experiments with young adult participants (age ranges 18-34, 18-35, 19-27, 20-42 years) and one experiment with school adolescents (approx. 17 years old). All participants were native Swedish speakers with normal hearing and normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
participants.recruitment: University students were recruited and compensated with a small honorarium or cinema tickets. School adolescents participated in exchange for a cinema ticket.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Spoken word lists (50 monosyllable words, 11 words, or 7 nouns per list), spoken sentences (5 words each), and 8-10 minute spoken lectures. Stimuli were presented in various acoustic conditions: 1) with broadband background noise (S/N ratio 4 dB or +5 dB(A)), 2) with long reverberation time (RT 1.17s-1.84s) or short reverberation time (RT 0.3s-0.53s), or 3) control conditions (S/N ratio 27 dB or +29 dB(A), or anechoic/0s RT). Some word lists had many or few phonological neighbors. Acoustic conditions were either real (sound-insulated climate chamber, ordinary classrooms) or simulated (CATT-Acoustics 8.0).

measures.instrument: Number of correctly recalled words from lists (free recall, serial recall)
Number of correct answers and response times for identifying previously heard sentences
Number of open-ended questions answered correctly about lecture content
Reading Span test (TIPS battery) or Operation Span test (OSPAN)
Number of extra list errors (words not presented), inventions in OSPAN, prior-list intrusions in OSPAN, delayed intrusions in OSPAN
Number of incorrectly repeated words/sentences (as a check), or sentence repetition test

findings.consequent: Recall of words (stated words)
findings.mechanism: Increased effort for word identification leaves fewer cognitive resources for encoding and rehearsal, impairing memory.
findings.quote: The number of words correctly recalled was significantly lower in the noisy condition (mean = 8.50 and 11.03 for the Noise and Control condition, respectively, F(1,30) = 17.28; p < 0.01, η2 = 0.365).

findings.consequent: Recall of words (primacy and recency parts of list)
findings.mechanism: Noise impaired retrieval from longer-term store (primacy) and interfered with short-term storage/rehearsal (recency).
findings.quote: the noise effect had its major influence in the first and last part of the list. This was reflected in an interaction between condition and parts in the quadratic trend (F(1,30) = 6.99; p = 0.013, η2 = 0.189).

findings.consequent: Recall of words (stated words)
findings.mechanism: Long RT makes word identification more inefficient, leaving fewer resources for further processing and memory.
findings.quote: Significantly fewer stated words were recalled in the Long RT than in the Short RT condition (means = 12.97 and 10.78 respectively, F (1, 30) = 7.67, p=.01, η2 = .20.

findings.consequent: Recall of words (first two parts of list)
findings.mechanism: Long RT increases resource demands for item identification, reducing time for transfer to long-term storage and early consolidation.
findings.quote: recall of the first two parts of the list only was affected by RT. This was reflected in an interaction between condition and parts in the linear trend F (1, 30) = 10.16; p = .003, η2= .25.

findings.consequent: Extra list errors in word recall
findings.mechanism: Long RT leads to less efficient inhibitory control, resulting in more intrusions.
findings.quote: Extra list errors were significantly less frequent in the short than in the long RT condition (means: 2.2 and 3.1, z= 2.22, p = .03).

findings.consequent: Recognition of sentences (correct responses)
findings.quote: A two-way ANOVA (condition x presentation order) showed no significant difference between the conditions regarding the number of correct responses of Hagerman’s sentences.

findings.consequent: Response time for identifying irrelevant sentences
findings.mechanism: Long RT increases processing time for more demanding recognition tasks (e.g., sorting out irrelevant sentences).
findings.quote: when sentences were heard in the short RT condition the participants were faster to identify the sentences that not had been presented (Short RT M = 3.03 s, Long RT M = 3.42 s, F (1, 31) = 4.62, p = .04, η2 = .13).

findings.consequent: Performance in word recall and sentence recognition tasks (Long/Short RT conditions)
findings.quote: Contrary to expectations, reading span performance was unrelated to performance in both the word list and sentence task as well as to the effect of RT in these tests.

findings.consequent: Memory for spoken lectures
findings.mechanism: Poor listening conditions impair memory and learning, even if speech is intelligible, by increasing cognitive load.
findings.quote: The participants’ memory performance was worse when the lecture was heard in the noise condition (M = 2.68, SD = 1.64) than in the control condition (M = 3.45, SD = 1.76), as shown in Figure 1. A 2 (Noise condition: +5dB S/N ratio vs. +29dB S/N ratio) × 2 (Condition order: +5dB S/N ratio first vs. +29dB S/N ratio first) analysis of variance, with Noise condition as a within-subject variable and Condition order as a between-subject variable, revealed a significant difference between the two background conditions, F(1, 26) = 6.71, MSE = 1.23, p < .05, η2 = .20, observed power = .70, but no significant main effect of condition order and no interaction between these two variables.

findings.consequent: Memory for spoken lectures
findings.mechanism: Poor listening conditions impair memory and learning, even if speech is intelligible, by increasing cognitive load.
findings.quote: The participants’ memory performance was worse when the lecture was heard with a long reverberation time (M = 2.16, SD = 1.57) than in the short reverberation time condition (M = 4.00, SD = 2.03), as shown in Figure 2. A 2 (Reverberation condition: long vs. short reverberation time) × 2 (Condition order: long reverberation time first vs. short reverberation time first) analysis of variance, with Reverberation condition as a within-subject variable and Condition order as a between-subject variable, revealed a significant difference between the two reverberation conditions, F(1, 17) = 16.60, MSE = 2.12, p < .001, η2 = .49, observed power = .97

findings.consequent: Self-reported hearing of lectures
findings.quote: The participants’ mean rating of how well they heard the lecture was 4.95 (SD = 1.75) in the short reverberation time condition and 4.68 (SD = 1.89) in the long reverberation time condition. These two means did not differ significantly, as shown by a paired t-test, t(18) < 1.

findings.quote: A 3(Reverberation time) × 8(serial position) analysis of variance revealed no effect of Reverberation time, F(2, 58) = 1.46, MSE = 5.03, p = 0.24

findings.quote: but an effect of serial position, F(7, 203) = 66.16, MSE = 4.96, p < 0.01.

mechanisms: Degraded speech signals (low S/N ratio or long reverberation time) increase the cognitive load required for speech identification, transforming an automatic bottom-up process into a resource-demanding top-down process.

Increased cognitive effort for speech perception reduces the cognitive resources available for higher-order cognitive processes such as encoding, rehearsal, chunking, and elaboration, thereby impairing memory performance.

Degraded speech signals activate more phonological candidates in the mental lexicon, leading to increased competition for word identification and requiring greater inhibitory control to suppress irrelevant candidates.
Inefficient inhibitory control, particularly in individuals with lower working memory capacity, results in more false recalls and intrusions from activated non-target words.

The temporal distinctiveness of items in a list influences recall, with mid-list items being less distinctive and potentially more vulnerable to interference from activated phonological neighbors in degraded conditions.
The effect of degraded stimuli on memory is primarily due to memory impairment rather than missed identification, as evidenced by interactions between condition and serial position.
moderators: Working memory capacity (measured by reading span or operation span, including sub-measures like inventions and delayed intrusions)
Serial position of words in a list (primacy, mid, recency)
implementation_implications: Acoustical conditions in buildings designed for communication and learning (e.g., classrooms, conference rooms) should be evaluated based on memory criteria, not solely on speech intelligibility criteria.

Standards for acceptable S/N ratios and reverberation times should be more stringent to ensure that spoken information can be heard without special effort, which is crucial for proper learning and memory.

Building standards should be updated to consider the cognitive load imposed by poor acoustics, especially for vulnerable populations like older people and young children, and those with hearing impairment or non-native language backgrounds.

limitations: All studies were performed with young adult participants, limiting generalizability to older people, young children, or individuals with hearing impairment or different language backgrounds.
The use of a repetition procedure for word identification in some studies might have led to better recall performance, potentially underestimating the true effects of degraded listening conditions.

No consistent relation was found between working memory capacity and the learning effect in unfavorable listening conditions across all studies, suggesting the need for more reliable measures of WMC for cognitively demanding listening conditions.
